refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: systemd-machine-id-setup may be used by system installer tools to initialize the machine ID stored in /etc/machine-id at install time, with a provisioned or randomly generated ID. See machine-id5 for more information about this file.

If the tool is invoked without the --commit switch, /etc/machine-id is initialized with a valid, new machine ID if it is missing or empty. The new machine ID will be acquired in the following fashion:

listitem.para: If a valid machine ID is stored in /run/machine-id, the machine ID is copied and used to initialize the machine ID in /etc/machine-id. This step is skipped if --root= is specified or running in a chroot environment.
If a valid D-Bus machine ID is already configured for the system, the D-Bus machine ID is copied and used to initialize the machine ID in /etc/machine-id.

If a valid machine ID is provided through system.machine_id credential, the machine ID is copied and used to initialize the machine ID in /etc/machine-id. This step is skipped if --root= is specified or running in a chroot environment.

If run inside a KVM virtual machine and a UUID is configured (via the -uuid option), this UUID is used to initialize the machine ID. The caller must ensure that the UUID passed is sufficiently unique and is different for every booted instance of the VM. This step is skipped if --root= is specified or running in a chroot environment.

Similarly, if run inside a Linux container environment and a UUID is configured for the container, this is used to initialize the machine ID. For details, see the documentation of the Container Interface. This step is skipped if --root= is specified or running in a chroot environment.
Otherwise, a new ID is randomly generated.

refsect1.para: The --commit switch may be used to commit a transient machined ID to disk, making it persistent. For details, see below.

The --force switch adds to this: it may be used to assign a completely new identity to a system that already carries a valid machine ID, for example after cloning a disk image. A missing or empty /etc/machine-id is initialized as described above either way, except that the first two sources of that list — /run/machine-id and the D-Bus machine ID — are skipped: the former holds the identity a booted clone is currently using, the latter the one baked into the image. The refusals described below apply to those cases too. For details, see below.
Use systemd-firstboot1 to initialize the machine ID on mounted (but not booted) system images.

listitem.para: Takes a directory path as argument. All paths operated on will be prefixed with the given alternate root path, including the path for /etc/machine-id itself.
Takes a path to a device node or regular file as argument. This is similar to --root= as described above, but operates on a disk image instead of a directory tree.

Commit a transient machine ID to disk. This command may be used to convert a transient machine ID into a persistent one. A transient machine ID file is one that was bind mounted from a memory file system (usually tmpfs) to /etc/machine-id during the early phase of the boot process. This may happen because /etc/ is initially read-only and was missing a valid machine ID file at that point.

This command will execute no operation if /etc/machine-id is not mounted from a memory file system, or if /etc/ is read-only. The command will write the current transient machine ID to disk and unmount the /etc/machine-id mount point in a race-free manner to ensure that this file is always valid and accessible for other processes.
This command is primarily used by the systemd-machine-id-commit.service8 early boot service.

Generate a new machine ID even if /etc/machine-id already contains a valid one, replacing it. This is useful to give a fresh identity to a system that was installed by cloning a disk image or a virtual machine, where all clones would otherwise share the machine ID baked into the image.

Contrary to the regular operation described above, the new ID is always generated from the random pool: none of the other sources are consulted, since on a cloned system they typically still carry the very ID that is supposed to be replaced. Those of them that are plain files inside the target tree — /run/machine-id and /var/lib/dbus/machine-id — are rewritten with the new ID, so that they cannot hand the old one back later. Symlinks among them are left untouched. This is best-effort: a copy that exists but cannot be written is reported as a warning and does not affect the exit status, so check the output if it matters. A copy that is simply absent — for instance because the clone's /var/ is not mounted under --root= — is indistinguishable from there being nothing to update and is not reported at all.

Since assigning a persistent identity is the point, the switch refuses to operate whenever the new ID would not actually stick, rather than falling back to a transient machine ID the way the regular operation does. This applies to every --force invocation, including the empty or missing case: if /etc/machine-id cannot be written to, or if it is a mount point, in which case the new ID would be written through the overmount instead of being persisted (if a transient ID was installed over it at boot, use --commit first; a container runtime bind-mounting the host's file into the tree lands here too).

Two further conditions are checked only when operating on the host, as they are not knowable for a tree given with --root= or --image=. The switch refuses if systemd.machine_id= on the kernel command line carries an ID that would take precedence on the next boot (a value of firmware, or no value at all, does not, and is accepted), and if /etc/machine-id itself resides on a temporary file system such as tmpfs (note this follows the symlink, so a symlinked /etc/machine-id is judged by its target). The latter cannot detect every volatile setup: with systemd.volatile=overlay /etc/ is an overlayfs whose upper layer is volatile, which is indistinguishable from an overlayfs with a persistent upper layer.

If /etc/machine-id contains the string uninitialized it is left alone, even with this switch: that state carries no identity that could have been duplicated by cloning, and doubles as the first boot marker, see machine-id5. To assign an ID right away regardless, use systemd-firstboot1 as systemd-firstboot --root=… --force --setup-machine-id, which generates a random one, or --machine-id= to pick it yourself. Its own --force is required because the file already exists; note that it also lifts the --root=/--image= requirement that systemd-firstboot1 documents for these switches, so the same command works on a running system.

Be aware that this writes /etc/machine-id directly: none of the checks described here apply, and stale copies in /run/machine-id and /var/lib/dbus/machine-id are left carrying whatever they held — on a clone, that is the identity of the image it came from.

Note that this only updates the machine ID on disk. Programs that already obtained the machine ID — including the service manager itself — keep using the old one, hence the system should be rebooted for the new ID to take effect. Also note that changing the machine ID discards or invalidates state keyed by it, some of it irreversibly; see the "Cloned Systems" section of machine-id5 for the full list, and review it before using this switch.
This switch may not be combined with --commit.
Print the machine ID generated or committed after the operation is complete.

refsect1.title: Exit status
refsect1.para: On success, 0 is returned, a non-zero failure code otherwise.
